articles.title: State judicial races are on the ballot in November. Here’s what you need to know
articles.summary: The midterms are not just about Congress. While high-profile contests that will determine the balance of power in Washington have dominated news cycles, judicial elections are also happening in half of the country on Nov. 3. State Supreme Court races are on the ballot in 24 states, with half of those being retention elections in which voters decide whether an incumbent judge should remain…
articles.body:
The midterms are not just about Congress.

While high-profile contests that will determine the balance of power in Washington have dominated news cycles, judicial elections are also happening in half of the country on Nov. 3.

State Supreme Court races are on the ballot in 24 states, with half of those being retention elections in which voters decide whether an incumbent judge should remain seated for another term. More than 200 seats on appellate court benches and even more at the trial-court level are also up, according to Ballotpedia .

These races often get overshadowed, but their outcomes are influential.

“Issues that reach the state Supreme Court affect every corner of [people’s] lives,” said American University professor Thomas Kahn, naming them as among the “most powerful courts in the land,” second only to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Douglas Keith, the deputy director of the Brennan Center for Justice’s judiciary program, noted that 95 percent of all cases each year are filed outside of the federal court system.

“There may have been cases that the public thought previously would always end up at the U.S. Supreme Court, but now they’re going to go to and end at their state’s highest court, and that could be case about abortion rights or voting rights or environmental law or criminal justice reform,” he said. “All of these things are issues that state high courts have a tremendous amount of power to interpret and apply.”

The process for putting a judge on the state Supreme Court bench varies in each state, which is why not every voter sees them on the ballot at the same time — if at all.

The Brennan Center notes that elections are used as at least part of the judicial selection system in 38 states , through a combination of partisan, nonpartisan and retention elections. The remaining states use gubernatorial or direct legislative appointments, though the exact methods differ.

Contested races are generally conducted like any other election for political office. And depending on the state, candidates may or may not have a party label attached to their names on the ballot.

Retention states are different. A justice, usually appointed by the governor, has no opponent and faces a simple yes-or-no vote on whether they should keep their job. And it’s rare for judges to lose them.

“It’s not unprecedented, but it does not happen often,” Kahn said.

Partisan contests for state Supreme Courts are concentrated in just a handful of states, only some of which still have races to decide in November.

In Alabama, Democrat AshLeigh Dunham is running against Republican incumbent Greg Shaw for a spot on the highest court. North Carolina will see Democratic incumbent Anita Earls square off against Republican Sarah Stevens.

Ohio voters are electing justices for two Supreme Court seats, with incumbent Democrat Jennifer Brunner facing Republican Colleen O’Donnell in the race for one, and incumbent Republican Dan Hawkins up against Democrat Marilyn Zayas in the other.

Four Republican justices — Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock and Associate Justices James Sullivan, Kyle Hawkins and Brett Busby — are seeking reelection in Texas, with each facing a Democratic challenger.

There are also two state Supreme Court seats on the ballot in Michigan, which uses a unique method to determine who’s on the ballot. Political parties select candidates during nominating conventions to compete against incumbents, but the general elections are nonpartisan, so those affiliations do not appear on the ballot.

And while seven other states are also holding nonpartisan state Supreme Court elections on paper, none are devoid of political influence.

“In states where the court’s ideological balance is nevertheless clear, and seemingly up for grabs, you will see interest groups that are clearly on the left or clearly on the right getting involved in these races to try and change the majority on the court,” Keith said.

“And so, just because a state has nonpartisan judicial elections does not mean those races won’t become highly politicized or very high cost,” he added.

That tension is at the center of an ongoing debate over whether judges, who are expected to apply the law evenly and impartially, should even have to campaign for office in the first place.

Supporters of the elections model argue that it gives voters a direct say in holding those in power accountable. But others say an appointment model better preserves judicial independence because it insulates judges from political pressure.

“There is no perfect way to pick judges, and these different systems all reflect an attempt to balance some values that are often competing like transparency and democratic accountability and quality of judges and all these things,” Keith noted.

The debate was put to the test in Kansas this year when voters overwhelmingly rejected a constitutional amendment in the August primary that would have allowed direct elections of state Supreme Court justices. That proposal was backed by Republicans, who have been pushing for more conservative rulings on issues like abortion and school funding, according to the Kansas Reflector .

As a result, the state’s retention elections will go ahead as planned in November, with Justices Larkin Walsh and Eric Rosen on the ballot.

In addition to selecting a replacement for a retiring justice on the state Supreme Court, voters in Montana are also considering a proposal that would enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution after the GOP-controlled Legislature failed to advance bills that would have made them partisan.

The push for partisanship in Montana reflects the “gamesmanship” going on behind the scenes in other states as well, Keith said.

“Legislators are doing everything they can to make these courts more of an ally and less of an obstacle,” he said. He pointed to both Montana and North Carolina as states where the ideological balance may not be at stake this year but will be in 2028.

Those who argue that states should stop electing judges say the influx of cash in these races is a big reason why.

A Politico poll conducted in April found that 72 percent of Americans said there was too much money in politics , with a majority saying they think money shapes election outcomes. Just less than 40 percent of respondents said money could outright buy results, while another 34 percent said money could influence elections but not buy them.

“In many cases … special interest money is being donated with the hope that the money may influence the outcome or the decisions of the judges, and of course, that’s a terrible result,” Kahn said. “You want judges to make decisions based just on the facts and on the merits and on the law, not on purely partisan political basis.”

That concern has long existed in state judicial races, as a Brennan Center poll indicates that a whopping 87 percent of voters in 2013 said they believed that campaign spending had “some” or “a great deal” of influence on judges’ decisionmaking.

Since then, hundreds of millions of dollars have continued to flood into these contests.

More than $100 million was estimated to have been spent on last year’s officially nonpartisan Wisconsin Supreme Court race between Susan Crawford and Brad Schimel, attracting mega-donors like Elon Musk and George Soros, along with their affiliated PACs.

And while spending isn’t expected to reach close to that level in any race this cycle, data still shows campaign advertising figures in the thousands to low millions across several states.

“If courts are supposed to be doing something different than raw politics, all of this spending and the more these races look like any other elected office, make it much harder for the public to think of judges as anything other than politicians in robes,” Keith said.

Further down the ballot are also elections for seats on appellate court benches. These judges are usually the first to hear appeals of trial court decisions, and because high courts hear only a small share of cases, they often effectively have the final say on how to interpret state law.

Keith acknowledges that obtaining information about judicial races is “harder than it should be.” He recommends that voters take advantage of guides from state bar associations and voting rights groups and seek the perspective of lawyers and advocates who are familiar with the workings of the state’s legal system before choosing whom to vote for.

“To me, this is one of the key unresolved tensions in the decision to elect judges,” he said. “It is one thing to adopt a system that allows for some amount of democratic accountability but that assumes that you are giving the public enough information to sort of carry out that accountability.”

“And as of yet, I don’t think that the public is being given the information that they deserve or are entitled to in order to make those decisions.”

articles.title: Candy prices surge beyond inflation, but Americans still plan to spend billions on Halloween staples
articles.summary: Candy prices rose 7.7% over the past year, but Halloween shoppers are expected to spend $4.1 billion on sweets using coupons and sales strategies.
articles.body: Trick-or-treating, like most expenses recently, will come with a bigger price tag this Halloween. The increase is hitting as families prepare for a holiday built around candy. Shoppers, however, still plan to spend billions on Halloween treats, even as rising prices make affordability part of the seasonal calculation. Candy prices rose 7.7% over the year through September, more than twice the overall inflation rate of 3.7%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure tracks candy and chewing gum broadly, rather than Halloween-specific products. But higher prices haven’t pushed candy out of the Halloween budget. The National Retail Federation expects Americans to spend $4.1 billion on candy this year as part of a record $13.5 billion in overall Halloween spending. Its survey found that 96% of Halloween shoppers plan to buy sweets. "Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind," NRF Vice President of Industry and Consumer Insights Allison Zeller said. THE FAMILY BEHIND AN ICONIC AMERICAN FAIR FOOD REVEALS THE SECRET TO ITS STAYING POWER The NRF found that 31% of shoppers plan to comparison shop if prices are higher than expected, while 26% will look for coupons or sales. Retailers are offering products across a range of price points to help shoppers celebrate within their budgets, Zeller said. NIQ said rising costs for housing, transportation and everyday essentials are shaping spending decisions, but Halloween remains an occasion consumers are willing to protect. That resilience showed up in last year’s sales. Halloween confectionery sales rose 7.6% in 2025 even as unit sales fell 2.5%, suggesting shoppers spent more while taking home fewer items. Chocolate had the largest average unit-price increase among the confectionery categories NIQ tracked, at 11.5%. YOUR SUMMER BBQ IS ABOUT TO COST MORE – HERE’S THE SURPRISING REASON WHY "Consumers continue to make room for Halloween. What’s changing is how they participate," said Chris Costagli, NIQ’s vice president of food and beverage thought leadership. Shoppers are starting earlier, spreading purchases across more trips and evaluating items more carefully, he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The National Confectioners Association said candy makers and retailers offer seasonal promotions and different package sizes to give shoppers options at various price points.

articles.title: US has plans for major Iran strikes if Trump chooses
articles.summary: US forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch new, potentially major, military operations against Iran “within 96 hours of receiving” an order from Pre...
articles.body:
US forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch new, potentially major, military operations against Iran "within 96 hours of receiving" an order from President Donald Trump, according to two US officials.

Sufficient forces are now deployed in the region to carry out the potential attacks, the sources said. The scope of new US military operations would likely go beyond efforts to simply "mow the lawn" or maintain the status quo by striking radars, launchers and other Iranian assets that can be quickly reconstituted — as has been the case since Trump halted full combat operations earlier this year, the sources added.

"It will be a big effort," one of the officials told CNN. That view has been echoed by other current and former US officials familiar with internal military planning discussions — some of whom say it is a question of when, not if, Trump will issue a go-order. They believe it could come any time before the end of the year, though most likely after the US midterm elections.

US officials acknowledge challenges, cite potential threat

Iranian forces are now more familiar with US tactics, and it would therefore be harder for the American military to effectively destroy all potential intended targets. However, leaders in US Central Command and the Pentagon have been developing a wide-ranging target list, which includes Iranian energy infrastructure, military sites and nuclear facilities.

Officials say that Trump has not made up his mind on what he will do after the midterms but that he appears to be leaning toward ordering major action. But officials also caution that Trump has appeared in the past to lean toward certain actions only to back off at the last moment.

A senior Pentagon official told CNN in a statement, "The Department is a planning organization, and its job is to develop and execute military options ordered by the President."

Recent US intelligence assessments indicate Iran and Houthi rebels are taking the possibility of renewed attacks by the US and potentially Israel very seriously, according to two additional sources familiar with the matter.

If the US and Israel launch new military operations against Iran, Tehran and the Houthis would likely retaliate immediately by targeting American personnel and facilities around the region — and potentially beyond, the sources familiar with those recent US intelligence assessments said.

An unclassified October 23 memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says US intelligence has found that "Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" and plotting efforts "have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," CNN previously reported .

US intelligence officials believe Iran and the Houthis are unlikely to carry out preemptive escalatory attacks against American personnel or Israel at this point but would not hesitate to respond if Iran is targeted first by US or Israeli forces, one of the sources familiar with the latest American intelligence assessments noted.

But the regional threat posed by Iran and the Houthis is one reason why the US is expected to continue quietly pulling personnel from its embassies across the Middle East in the coming days, the source said.

While the US Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is the only American diplomatic facility in the region under ordered departure , one of the sources told CNN that others are expected to receive similar directives and those that do not will be scaled down under a personnel cap.

Additionally, nonessential US military personnel who were expected to deploy to the Middle East as part of the next troop rotation have been told they are no longer being sent, according to a US official, underscoring the possibility of looming regional escalation.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, visited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as the US military maintains its blockade on Iranian ports and assists shipping traffic through the critical waterway.

Cooper "observed the current operational environment" while flying over the strait in a helicopter, CENTCOM said, adding that he met with service members who cleared the waterway of Iranian mines.

"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," Cooper said in a news release. "This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."

Despite the increase in tankers transiting the strait, oil prices remain high, partly due to the threat of possible Iranian attacks. One US official acknowledged the status quo around the strait is "untenable" for the long term, and barring a last-minute diplomatic breakthrough, is one reason Trump may turn to military action — despite questions about whether the White House has a broader strategy for ending the conflict.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing to carry out new attacks against Iran, but US officials have requested he delay until the Trump administration is ready to conduct joint operations, according to two US officials and an Israeli security source.

"Netanyahu really wanted and tried to convince Trump for a joint attack in Iran before the elections, and Trump did not give a green light," the Israeli security source told CNN. The prime minister's office said this was "fake news."

One reason Trump declined is because Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Eyal Zamir told US Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, that it would harm the elections in Israel and lead to their postponement, the Israeli security source added.

Israel's Channel 12 News reported Sunday there was an "unprecedented" confrontation between Zamir and Netanyahu fewer than 48 hours before Tuesday's vote. According to the report, Zamir received a directive from the political echelon related to Iran but requested an in-depth discussion and legal authorizations before carrying it out, fearing the action could lead to a miscalculation that could trigger an immediate conflict.

Defense Minister Israel Katz said the report was "completely baseless and false."

Israel was preparing for the possibility of launching additional attacks against Iran in the last week or so and had been lobbying US officials to support and complement those new strikes, a third source briefed on the matter told CNN. But senior US officials — including Trump — told Israel to hold off, instead signaling the two countries would launch joint operations soon.

Israel appears to have delayed plans in the immediate term for additional strikes but is building up for potential joint operations with the US — likely after the American midterm elections, all of the sources said.

Israel seemed to agree to delaying new strikes on Iran in part because it needs US support for missile defense, the source briefed on the matter added. Iran and the Houthis would likely retaliate against an attack and Israel's defensive munitions have been strained during the war.

Recent US intelligence assessments indicate that Netanyahu and his allies still lack a clear strategic objective beyond demonstrating some sort of "progress" and continuing to degrade the Iranian regime, one of the sources familiar with the reports added.

Netanyahu said this week in a speech at an IDF graduation ceremony that his directive to the IDF, the Mossad and other security branches is to topple the regime in Iran.

"The plans are ready, waiting for Trump's approval, could be after the midterms," the same source told CNN.

This story has been updated with additional developments Monday.

CNN's Kevin Liptak contributed to this report.

articles.title: $800-a-day penalty threatens to bleed reporter dry as explosive legal fight heads to Supreme Court
articles.summary: Catherine Herridge's Supreme Court petition challenges how courts weigh reporter's privilege when confidential national security sources are at stake.
articles.body: Former Fox News investigative reporter Catherine Herridge is asking the Supreme Court to protect her confidential sources after a federal court ordered her to identify who helped expose a woman's alleged ties to China's military. The outcome of the case could dramatically reshape the legal protections afforded to journalists working in the U.S. under the First Amendment. Herridge was held in contempt and ordered to pay $800 per day for refusing to reveal sources behind her 2017 reporting on Yanping Chen, a Chinese American businesswoman who operated a university attended by U.S. military personnel. Her reporting raised questions about Chen's alleged past as a colonel for the People's Liberation Army (PLA) of China and the potential exposure of sensitive information about American service members. The Department of War subsequently cut off military tuition assistance funding to Chen's university following a national security review, according to a filing by Herridge's legal team. The school had been receiving approximately $200,000 a month in taxpayer-funded tuition assistance. NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES Now Chen, who was investigated by federal authorities but never charged with a crime, is pursuing a lawsuit against the federal government, alleging that officials improperly disclosed her private records to Herridge in violation of the Privacy Act. She has sought to compel Herridge to identify her sources as part of that litigation. The dispute has reached the Supreme Court, where Herridge's attorneys are asking the justices to reconsider the legal standard used to force journalists to disclose confidential sources in civil cases. Her legal team argues that the lower courts failed to adequately weigh the broader circumstances of Chen's lawsuit, including the Pentagon's national security findings and whether Chen can ultimately prevail in her claims against the government. The case also exposes a longstanding disagreement among federal appeals courts over the scope of the reporter's privilege, an issue the Supreme Court has not comprehensively addressed in more than five decades. Herridge's original investigation, published while she was working at Fox News in 2017, examined Chen's background and her operation of the University of Management and Technology in Arlington, Virginia, which enrolled U.S. military personnel using Defense Department tuition assistance. The reporting included photographs appearing to show Chen in a Chinese military uniform and examined allegations that she had concealed her previous military service when applying for U.S. immigration benefits. It also raised concerns about the university's collection of information on American service members, including details about their military training and professional backgrounds. A whistleblower interviewed for the investigation alleged that information stored on the school's computers could be accessed remotely from China. WASHINGTON POST BOASTS IT STARED DOWN ‘UNWARRANTED’ JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUBPOENA Federal authorities had previously investigated Chen over potential immigration violations and counterintelligence concerns, but prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia declined to bring charges. Following Herridge's reporting, the Pentagon completed a review of Chen's university and terminated its eligibility for military tuition assistance funding, according to her filing. Chen subsequently filed suit against the federal government, alleging that confidential information from government records had been improperly disclosed to Herridge. She contends that identifying the officials responsible for the alleged disclosures is necessary to establish her Privacy Act claims. Herridge refused to identify her sources, arguing that compelling disclosure would undermine the ability of journalists to obtain sensitive information from government officials and whistleblowers. A federal judge ultimately ordered Herridge to disclose the sources and held her in civil contempt when she refused. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the order, prompting her appeal to the Supreme Court. Fox News Media has continued to support Herridge's legal fight, including covering her legal fees, despite her departure from the network in 2019. At the center of Herridge's petition is a disagreement among federal appeals courts over how judges should evaluate a journalist's claim of privilege when confidential sources are sought in civil litigation. The filing argues that the D.C. Circuit applied a narrow test focused primarily on whether Chen needed the information to pursue her lawsuit and whether she had exhausted alternative means of obtaining it. They contend that courts should also consider the strength of the underlying lawsuit and the consequences of compelling disclosure, particularly when confidential national security sources may be involved. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The distinction could prove significant for journalists reporting on sensitive government matters. Under the standard challenged by Herridge, a plaintiff could obtain a reporter's confidential sources even if other deficiencies in the lawsuit would ultimately prevent the plaintiff from recovering damages, according to the petition.

articles.title: Dem Senate hopeful rejects Schumer but benefits from millions in spending by his allies
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton distances himself from Chuck Schumer even as Senate Majority PAC pours millions into the Kansas Senate race against Roger Marshall.
articles.body: WICHITA, Kan. — National Democrats are pouring millions of dollars into Kansas to bolster Adam Hamilton, who has spent much of his campaign arguing that he would not be beholden to the top Democratic leaders in Washington, D.C. Tens of millions are flowing into Kansas to boost Hamilton, with a sizable chunk coming from Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC closely aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., whom Hamilton has repeatedly said he would not support as the Democratic leader should he win in November. But his opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., questioned how he could benefit from "$30 to $40 million from Chuck Schumer and not be beholden to him in some way?" THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES "Regardless of what he says, if we lose this seat, then it's going to give the Senate control to the Democrats," Marshall told Fox News Digital during an interview on the campaign trail. "Chuck Schumer would be the leader of the Senate." "Look, if he's going to denounce Chuck Schumer, let's denounce him with his money as well," he continued, "Look, we're going to be outspent five to one, and we knew that." Candidates, notably, can’t directly accept outside funding from independent groups like the Senate Majority PAC, given the guardrails are established by federal election law, according to the Federal Election Commission. SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL The Schumer-aligned group teed up $5 million in advertising spending in Kansas earlier this month, a sign that Democrats are bullish about flipping the seat in a contest that has gotten closer than Republicans expected. Hamilton's campaign pushed back on Marshall, arguing that the first-term senator has been given a lifeboat by national Republicans. Hamilton has vastly outraised Marshall, scoring nearly $14 million compared to Marshall’s almost $6 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings. "Adam has said repeatedly he believes it’s time for fresh leadership in Washington," Tyson Brody, a Hamilton campaign spokesperson, told Fox News Digital. "Adam will always put Kansas first. Meanwhile, Roger Marshall is totally dependent on Washington money to save his campaign because he has abandoned Kansas to support D.C. corruption, endless war and high prices." KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’ In all, national Democrats and their affiliated groups — combined with spending from Hamilton’s campaign — are slated to dump $38 million into the race, according to AdImpact. National Republicans, along with Marshall’s campaign, are putting $32 million into the contest. Marshall has sought to tie Hamilton, who is running as a moderate in ruby-red Kansas, directly to Schumer, a point he made several times during their final debate before Election Day this week. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamilton pushed back, arguing that Marshall had mentioned Schumer "maybe 20 times so far." "I’ve already said I wouldn't support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats took control of the Senate," Hamilton said.

articles.title: La edad de jubilación que propone Frente Amplio y que variaría el modelo actual: las diferencias
articles.standfirst: Propone fijarla en los 65 años y garantizar pensiones iguales o superiores al salario mínimo
articles.summary: Propone fijarla en los 65 años y garantizar pensiones iguales o superiores al salario mínimo
articles.body: Frente Amplio ha puesto sobre la mesa dos medidas clave en materia de pensiones en sus propuestas electorales: recuperar de forma efectiva la jubilación a los 65 años y garantizar que ninguna prestación quede por debajo del Salario Mínimo Interprofesional (SMI), situado actualmente en 1.221 euros mensuales. La formación de izquierdas ha defendido estas propuestas en defensa del sistema público de pensiones, convocada por la Coordinadora Estatal por la Defensa del Sistema Público de Pensiones (COESPE). En ese contexto, también ha cargado contra PP y Vox, a quienes acusa de impulsar políticas orientadas a recortar las prestaciones de los jubilados. La candidata de Frente Amplio a la Presidencia del Gobierno, Ada Colau, ha defendido que las pensiones deben evolucionar al mismo ritmo que el SMI. "Si estamos subiendo el salario mínimo porque el coste de la vida no deja de aumentar, lo lógico es que las pensiones también crezcan al mismo ritmo", señaló. Además, Colau reclamó que se establezca de forma "clara y contundente" que la edad máxima de jubilación sea de 65 años. Según explicó, en los últimos años la edad real y efectiva de retiro se ha ido retrasando progresivamente por encima de ese umbral. La coalición recordó también algunos datos sobre la situación actual de los pensionistas en España. Según expuso en un comunicado, 4,6 millones de jubilados cobran una pensión inferior al SMI, mientras que cerca de dos millones perciben menos de 900 euros al mes. Además, dos de cada tres mujeres pensionistas no alcanzan los 1.000 euros mensuales. Con estas propuestas, Frente Amplio busca convertir las pensiones en uno de los ejes de su programa electoral de cara a la cita con las urnas. aprobada por el Gobierno, la cual culminará en 2027 estableciendo la edad de retiro general en los 67 años. • A los 65 años: Te puedes jubilar si has cotizado 38 años y 3 meses o más. • A los 66 años y 10 meses: Es la edad ordinaria si tienes menos de 38 años y 3 meses cotizados. • Previsión para 2027: La edad legal general aumentará a 67 años

articles.title: Alaska Dem Senate candidate suffers minor injuries in car crash, forcing her to skip campaign events
articles.summary: Democratic Senate-nominee Mary Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries in an Anchorage crash, delaying her campaign tour in the Alaska Senate race.
articles.body: Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola and members of her family were involved in a two-vehicle collision in Anchorage on Saturday night, prompting her campaign to adjust upcoming schedule commitments in the final stretch of the midterm race. The crash occurred Saturday in the vicinity of the Alaska Federation of Natives (AFN) convention, where candidate events and campaign appearances had been underway over the weekend. It happened when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, the campaign said. The family was on their way to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet. "Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement. "Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover." "Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families," Bruce added. TODD BLANCHE CHALLENGES DANA BASH FOR ONLY CITING PART OF CONSTITUTION DURING HEATED ELECTION CLASH The pause comes at a pivotal moment in Alaska’s high-stakes Senate contest between Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, as both campaigns scramble across the state to mobilize voters and secure turnout ahead of the November midterm vote. DEMOCRAT'S DEBATE 'CUE CARDS' STEAL SPOTLIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE CLASH Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both she and Sullivan have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation. ALASKA HAS A VOTING SYSTEM LIKE NO OTHER STATE; REPUBLICANS WORRY IT COULD COST THEM IN NOVEMBER President Donald Trump — who held a rally in support of Sullivan earlier this month — said Friday he told his administration to sue to block certification of the race if the incumbent loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another candidate who is listed on the ranked choice ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Alaska allows voters to rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate. Voters will have four choices, including Sullivan, Peltola and the other Dan Sullivan, a candidate Republicans have called a decoy in what they believe is a Democratic effort to confuse voters. COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’ "I revealed what everyone knows, that the Ranked Choice Voting Ballot is a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.," Trump wrote early Sunday morning on Truth Social. "He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election." It is a reason to vote out ranked-choice voting, Trump added. "The Democrats are trying to steal this important Republican Seat and, if that happens, everything we’ve done for Alaska will come to an immediate hault [sic]," Trump concluded. "VOTE 'YES' AGAINST RANKED CHOICE VOTING, on Ballot Measure 2. SAVE ALASKA!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Peltola has outraised Sullivan through October, $33 million to nearly $14 million, but Sullivan reported having more campaign cash, $5.1 million to Peltola's $3.2 million. Republicans have outspent Democrats in the race, $42 million to $38 million. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Nicki Minaj acompaña en un mitin a Trump en el Air Force One y éste elogia su "culo precioso": "Es difícil no verlo"
articles.standfirst: La artista ha reforzado su vínculo con el movimiento conservador estadounidense y apoya al presidente en todo lo que puede
articles.summary: La artista ha reforzado su vínculo con el movimiento conservador estadounidense y apoya al presidente en todo lo que puede
articles.body: La relación entre Nicki Minaj y Donald Trump da muestras de una gran cordialidad y afinidad. La rapera trinitense acompañó este fin de semana al presidente de Estados Unidos a bordo del Air Force One rumbo a un acto de campaña celebrado en Michigan para respaldar al candidato republicano al Senado, Mike Rogers. La artista se ha convertido con el paso de los años en una de sus seguidoras más visibles. Su apoyo al mandatario ha quedado reflejado en diversas apariciones públicas junto a miembros de la Administración republicana. La última muestra de esa cercanía llegó a través de un vídeo compartido en X por Steven Cheung, director de comunicaciones de la Casa Blanca. En las imágenes, Minaj aparece dentro del avión presidencial alabando las políticas impulsadas por Trump. "Creo que hemos encontrado a la nueva secretaria de prensa de la Casa Blanca", bromeó Cheung en la publicación. La cantante respondió al comentario con un emoji de risa. Si bien Minaj no actuó en el mitin, pero sí estuvo apoyándolo con su presencia, fue el propio Trump el que quiso hacer un inciso al respecto. Y el presidente le dedicó un llamativo comentario al elogiar su "culo precioso". "Ponte de pie, es difícil no verlo", afirmó el mandatario ante el público. El evento tenía como principal objetivo impulsar la candidatura de Mike Rogers, que se enfrenta al demócrata Abdul El-Sayed en una disputada carrera por un escaño en el Senado. Los comicios de medio mandato del próximo 3 de noviembre serán clave para definir el control del Congreso estadounidense. En los últimos años, Minaj ha reforzado su vínculo con el movimiento conservador estadounidense. La cantante, que cuenta con millones de seguidores agrupados bajo el nombre de Barbz, ha llegado incluso a declararse como la "fan número uno" de Trump. El acercamiento resulta llamativo si se tiene en cuenta que en 2018 criticó duramente la política migratoria del republicano y reveló que había llegado a Estados Unidos de manera irregular cuando apenas tenía cinco años. Ya en enero de este año, aseguró haber recibido de forma gratuita una "tarjeta dorada" impulsada por Trump, un controvertido programa vinculado a la obtención de la residencia permanente para extranjeros que realizan importantes aportaciones económicas al Gobierno estadounidense.

articles.title: Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola pauses midterms campaigning after car crash
articles.summary: Mary Peltola, who suffered minor injuries, is running in one of the most closely watched races in the upcoming elections.
articles.body:
Mary Peltola, Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, has paused campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections after sustaining "minor injuries" in a car crash.

Peltola, 53, and her family were travelling to an event on Saturday when the vehicle they were in was hit by another driver, her campaign said in a statement.

She is running in one of the most closely watched races in the elections, which take place on 3 November - one that could help decide the balance of power in government.

Peltola has rescheduled campaign events "as she takes time to recover" on the advice of medical professionals, her campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, said in a statement.

"Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," Bruce said.

Peltola is trying to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has classified the Alaska senate race as a "toss-up", meaning neither the Republicans nor the Democrats hold a decisive advantage.

Trump told the justice department to file a federal lawsuit last week to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.

The suit said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.

Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.

articles.title: Mamdani message to residents on how to deal with ICE results in viral internet backlash: 'Treason'
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani's Spanish-language video on handling ICE encounters drew over 7 million views and fierce backlash from conservative lawmakers.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faced viral backlash on Friday after posting instructions in Spanish on how residents should handle interactions with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "If you encounter ICE, here's what every New Yorker should know," the socialist mayor of the nation’s largest city posted on X on Friday in a message that quickly racked up over 7 million views. Mamdani explained "what every New Yorker should know" if they "encounter ICE," adding that ICE "cannot enter private spaces like your home, school, hospitals or private areas of a workplace without a judicial warrant signed by a judge." Mamdani reminded New Yorkers they have the right to remain silent and gives tips on best practices for interacting with ICE, saying that "these are very frightening times for many people." MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION' Mamdani’s post was quickly criticized by conservatives on social media, with many characterizing the video as the mayor encouraging obstruction of federal law enforcement and encouraging illegal immigration. "It should be insulting to every American that the mayor of our largest city is a guy who became a citizen less than a decade ago and now spends his time coaching illegal aliens in a foreign language on how they can avoid being lawfully deported," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, posted on X. MULLIN CALLS MAMDANI'S ANTI-ICE RHETORIC 'DANGEROUS' FOLLOWING NEW YORK SHOOTING "Unless you're here illegally, you have no reason to fear ICE," actor Dean Cain posted on X. "This wanker is dangerous." "At no point in this video is anyone urged to abide by the laws of the United States," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, posted on X. "Because it was not made for the benefit of the people of the United States." "If you're here illegally, you're not a New Yorker," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted on X. "Period." "Treason," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, posted on X. "Here we are in 2026 with foreign born Democrats instructing illegals how to evade the law and remain in our country to suck off our system and best case scenario free load off our hard work," Fox News commentator Tomi Lahren posted on X. "Dangerous incitement full of disturbing falsehoods by communist terrorist supporter @NYCMayor," Judicial Watch President Tom Fitton posted on X. "This statement could put lives in danger." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment. Mamdani has repeatedly positioned himself against ICE and the Trump administration’s immigration-enforcement agenda. During his campaign and after taking office, he called for abolishing ICE and said the NYPD would not assist the agency with civil immigration enforcement. He has also described ICE operations as harmful to immigrant communities. As mayor, Mamdani signed an executive order strengthening New York City’s sanctuary policies. The order directs city agencies to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, protect personal information and establish protocols for handling ICE requests to access city property or records. It also called for expanded "know your rights" materials and training for city employees.

articles.title: Thousands of observers are expected to descend on polling places to monitor the vote on Election Day
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office.
articles.body: NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office. They won't be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times. The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy. The Democratic National Committee created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes, said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC. That's as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment. On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign. “We’ve never done this before,” Kleeb said of the party’s sweeping efforts. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.” The Department of Justice has already filed lawsuits in California and Alaska that could affect ballot counting or certification. While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed “radical Democrats” for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures. “President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections,” Bis said. Tens of thousands of volunteers trained to observe State Democratic parties have trained an estimated 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report anything potentially concerning they might see from federal agents. Common Cause has trained roughly 16,000 more volunteers to stand watch at voting precincts, said Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group. She said a broader Election Protection coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more. Smaller pockets of volunteers from other groups also are preparing to show up, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from a Democratic-allied group called Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other local community members. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks. There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations. Almeida said Election Day confusion is possible in some precincts but the nature of the threat requires a collective effort. “It will actually take all of us if some of the threats we are most worried about come to pass,” she said. Trump administration sends its own team Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump appointee who leads the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, was asked on CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether the Republican administration is planning to send ICE agents to polling places. “There is no plan to do that,” she responded. Still, the Justice Department is planning its largest-ever election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 department staff expected to observe voting and ensure federal laws are being followed, spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. That comes after a primary season in which the department said it deployed more than 100 election monitors across hundreds of polling locations. At least one of those placements sparked tensions with local officials. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, said the behavior of two monitors during that state's primary was “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” A Laramie County clerk said the Justice Department monitors arrived at the polls intending to interview voters, but her office didn’t allow it. The department disagrees that the monitors did anything improper, Pels said. She added that the monitors are trained to comply with federal law governing conduct at polling places and won’t “interfere with the voting process.” Democratic lawmakers and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that the Trump administration’s monitors could intimidate voters or abandon the duty they’ve had for decades to protect against civil rights violations. The department plans to send them to every state, focusing on high-population areas, jurisdictions that have had problems in the past and districts with close elections, according to a senior department official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity under terms set by the department. The Republican National Committee said its operation involves deploying “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina. Those workers are the “eyes and the ears of the RNC in the field” who recruit volunteers and organize trainings, said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. Their mission is to surface anything that seems unlawful. At the same time, the RNC has enlisted nearly 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll-watching volunteers for competitive districts. The poll watchers will “observe the process and help ensure election rules are followed in accordance with the law,” Triolo said. Local election officials prepare for increased attention While federal monitors have quietly observed elections for decades, largely without incident, some election officials are taking precautions. Chris Swope, the city clerk in Lansing, Michigan, said he preemptively contacted law enforcement and his attorney in case federal monitors violate election law, although he expects them to abide by the rules. The Democratic Mayors Association issued guidance to local Democratic officials with detailed instructions about what to do if federal agents appear at polling locations. It notes that federal law prohibits the presence of federal immigration agents, the FBI or other investigative personnel. It also issued a reminder that federal agents are not allowed to be armed at the polls, nor are they allowed to interact with voters or handle ballots or election equipment. Justice Department officials have said their monitors won't be armed and will not interfere with voting. Asked about department monitors being sent to Georgia, Trump told a reporter recently: “They’re not going to do anything other than watch." Some of the poll observations have already begun. Mary Corcoran, Save America's executive director, said her group's volunteers have been monitoring precincts during early voting in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio to help give voters a sense of security. “The fear is the point, and we must do something about it,” she said. “Left unanswered, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.” ___ Associated Press writers Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

articles.title: Inside House GOP's unprecedented push to monitor midterm elections and prepare for legal fights
articles.summary: House Republicans are sending dozens of congressional observers to monitor ballot counting in close midterm races and prepare for legal challenges.
articles.body: House Republicans are deploying "dozens and dozens" of staff across the country next Tuesday to ensure the midterm elections are being run cleanly and fairly as both parties fight tooth and nail for control of Congress. The Committee on House Administration, which has jurisdiction over federal elections, runs an annual election watcher program aimed at adding oversight in districts where races are anticipated to be particularly close, and in some cases, paving the way for legal challenges if improprieties are found. Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., the panel's chairman, told Fox News Digital that this year's program will be "the most robust program the House has ever done." "We're building on the success that we had last cycle and recognizing that a large number of House races are likely to be close," Steil said. "The balance of power in the United States House of Representatives is at stake, and we wanna make sure that we have eyes and ears on the ground in close races across the country." BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS VOTER-FRAUD PROBES IN BATTLEGROUND STATES JUST DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS How that plays out will vary from state to state depending on varying election laws, he explained. But many of those observers are potentially in for lengthy shifts. SENATE REPUBLICANS PUSH ELECTION DAY DEADLINE FOR CALIFORNIA'S MARATHON BALLOT COUNTS "Some jurisdictions that run their elections well, like Florida, their shift may end early in the evening. States that have kind of poor election policies, like California, those shifts go on for days on end until the counting is done," Steil said. "Two years ago, I went to Los Angeles County — about 10 million people — counts all their ballots at one location. And of course, we know California has bad election policy. They allow ballots to arrive after the polls have closed. And so I went to Central Count, met with our election observers as we watched ballots arrive days after the election. We want eyes and ears on the ground, recording what is occurring, and documenting what's happening, and making sure that the rules are followed." Steil also recalled an instance in Milwaukee where an issue arose during tabulation "where ultimately thousands of ballots would have to be recounted." But those poll watchers, trained under the jurisdiction of Congress, will often stay the entire time votes are being cast on Election Day. In some cases, they observe votes being counted as well. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY "These are long days. I mean, polling locations are often open for a full 12 hours. They're arriving, they're staying often until the early evening or late evening, in some cases as the ballots are actually tabulated, but they play an absolutely essential role in verifying... our elections are run freely and fairly," he said. It is all part of a process to build a case in the event the results need to be re-examined. Their documentation could potentially lead to recounts in close races or even lawsuits. "Not only are they documenting what they're seeing, but they're in direct contact with myself and the committee on Election Day, so that we're in a position to deploy additional resources, if necessary, to make any court challenges if that was required," Steil explained. "They are the first step in identifying if there is a problem, and then they notify our team and we get to work immediately." Election observers' jobs are federally protected under the Confirmation of Congressional Observer Access Act, which was enacted by Congress in 2024. The program is open to any staffer of the House of Representatives, save for interns. articles.title: Major school district's pledge with teachers' union sparks racial discrimination complaint
articles.summary: Defending Education filed a civil rights complaint alleging Cherry Creek Schools in Colorado discriminates by race in its teacher hiring policies.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: One of Colorado's largest school districts is facing a new federal civil rights complaint over a pledge it made with its teachers' union to recruit, retain and advance educators of color. Defending Education filed a federal civil rights complaint Monday, which was first obtained by Fox News Digital, with the U.S. Department of Education alleging that CCSD is discriminating on the basis of race in employment. CCSD is notably Colorado’s fourth-largest school district, and serves 52,000 students and more than 300,000 residents in the southeast Denver metropolitan area, according to the district’s website. At the heart of the complaint is the district's June 2023 "Educators of Color Declaration," which commits Cherry Creek School District and its teacher’s union to recruiting, retaining and advancing educators of color, even as a separate provision in the same agreement calls for recruitment, hiring and advancement to be based on qualifications without regard to race. "Cherry Creek Schools has written racial preferences directly into its teachers’ contract. The district’s ‘Educators of Color Declaration’ commits it to recruiting, retaining, and promoting teachers based on the color of their skin — which means other equally qualified teachers are passed over for the same reason," Sarah Parshall Perry, Vice President and Senior Legal Fellow at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital. "That's not diversity; it's discrimination, and it is precisely what Title VI and the Fourteenth Amendment forbid. The Supreme Court could not have been clearer in Students for Fair Admissions: the law is colorblind, and a school district cannot cure a race-based hiring policy with generic 'equal opportunity' language." Title VI prohibits race discrimination in federally funded programs under specified conditions, while Title VII more directly governs employment discrimination, leaving the legality of Cherry Creek's teacher recruitment and advancement commitments dependent on how those policies are implemented. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE CLEARS WAY FOR WHITE EMPLOYEE TO CHALLENGE SEATTLE'S DEI POLICIES The "Educators of Color Declaration" also commits the district and its teachers' union to intentionally recruiting highly qualified educators of color while making a concerted effort to retain those already employed by the district and help them advance into leadership positions, according to the district's negotiated agreement. JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY Additionally, the policy says that "to fulfill these goals, all policies in this agreement shall reflect Cherry Creek School District core values by grounding the work of negotiations in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)," according to the school district's 2026-2027 Negotiated Agreement. FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS "Cherry Creek is under no obligation to accept federal funding, but because it has, it cannot run a racial balancing scheme for its own workforce and still adhere to federal law," Perry continued. "We are asking the Office for Civil Rights to open an investigation and put an end to it." Defending Education's latest complaint comes after the Department of Education announced a separate investigation on June 8, into allegations that Cherry Creek School District sponsored racially discriminatory programs involving students, teachers and parents. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These allegations of racially discriminatory conduct in this District seem to permeate almost every aspect of the school community, affecting students, teachers, and parents alike," Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey said in a statement at the time. "Federal law prohibits racial discrimination, which means that race cannot be a factor in how the school educates its students or trains its teachers." The Trump administration has been cracking down on DEI efforts across the nation's education system, including proposing new regulations in September that would revoke the tax-exempt status of private schools and colleges that consider race in admissions, scholarships or other school-administered programs. CCSD did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on Monday. When reached for comment, a Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "the Department does not confirm complaints."
